info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 7.1: Collating Two Witnesses by Hand.

questiontext.text: What is the primary purpose of collating manuscript witnesses in textual scholarship?

generalfeedback.text: Collation records differences because differences are evidence about transmission — not for their own sake.

answer.text: To assemble a structured dataset of differences that serves as evidence for reconstructing textual transmission and descent.

feedback.text: Correct. Collation records differences not for their own sake, but because shared errors and omissions provide the evidential basis for inferring genealogical relationships.

answer.text: To create a comprehensive catalogue of every scribal spelling mistake for linguistic archiving.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Cataloguing variation for its own sake is not the goal; collation gathers evidence specifically to understand textual transmission.

answer.text: To prove that the earliest surviving manuscript is the most authentic witness.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Collation does not presuppose the priority of any witness; it gathers data to test hypotheses about descent.

answer.text: To automatically generate a definitive critical text without editorial intervention.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Collation produces the dataset of differences; establishing the text remains an interpretive editorial task.

questiontext.text: Why does collating against a single chosen base text introduce methodological bias?

generalfeedback.text: A base text privileges one witness's readings as the norm — with two witnesses this barely matters, and Wednesday's method avoids it entirely.

answer.text: Differences are recorded as deviations from the base, structurally privileging its readings as the norm and framing other witnesses as corruptions.

feedback.text: Correct. If the base happens to be a poor witness, superior readings in other witnesses are recorded merely as departures from a corrupt baseline.

answer.text: Comparing against a base text makes it mathematically impossible to calculate edit distances.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Edit distances can still be calculated; the problem is the structural privilege assigned to the chosen baseline.

answer.text: A base text requires editors to discard all orthographic and punctuation evidence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A base text can record any layer of variation; the bias concerns how differences are framed relative to one witness.

answer.text: Collation algorithms refuse to execute unless all witnesses are aligned simultaneously without a reference.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Many early computational programs were built explicitly around pairwise comparison against a master base text.

questiontext.text: Why is it standard practice to collate on the layer for the main critical apparatus while analyzing separately?

generalfeedback.text: Collate on for the substantive apparatus and analyze separately — one collation cannot serve both purposes.

answer.text: Collating on isolates substantive variants from orthographic noise, while preserves evidence of scribal habit and dialect.

feedback.text: Correct. Collating unnormalized text produces massive noise that buries substantive variants, but suppressing orthography entirely would discard valuable scribal evidence.

answer.text: TEI schemas prohibit encoding readings within an apparatus criticus.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI easily accommodates both layers; separating them is a methodological choice to maintain apparatus readability.

answer.text: Orthographic differences carry higher genealogical value than lexical substitutions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Orthographic variants are polygenetic and carry low stemmatic value compared to substantive lexical variants.

answer.text: Collation on produces diplomatic transcriptions, whereas produces normalized reading editions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That reverses the terms: represents diplomatic forms and represents regularized forms.

questiontext.text: When extracting text from TEI XML containing elements for collation, what happens if the unused layer is not removed before stripping tags?

generalfeedback.text: Remove the layer you are not collating before stripping markup, or every produces a token that matches nothing.

answer.text: Both and text are concatenated together into single nonsensical tokens that match nothing in other witnesses.

feedback.text: Correct. Stripping markup without removing the alternate element merges both layers into strings like τιμιτιμή, destroying alignment.

answer.text: The XML parser throws an unrecoverable validation error and halts extraction.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Regular expression or naive tag stripping does not fail with an XML error; it silently concatenates the text nodes.

answer.text: The extracted text automatically defaults to Unicode NFD normalization.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tag stripping does not alter Unicode normalization forms.

answer.text: Line break numbers are duplicated at every word boundary in the output.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The failure is token concatenation inside , not line number duplication.

name.text: 05 Question: Why Today Is on Paper

questiontext.text: Why is manual collation on paper pedagogically essential before attempting automated alignment?

generalfeedback.text: You will make dozens of tacit judgements today — the record of them, not the variant list, is what Wednesday needs.

answer.text: It forces the editor to become aware of the dozens of tacit philological decisions and discounting rules that an algorithm must be told explicitly.

feedback.text: Correct. Human readers normalize effortlessly and silently; working on paper slows the process down so implicit rules can be captured as configuration.

answer.text: Paper collation is faster and less prone to fatigue than computational alignment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manual collation is slow and highly fatiguing; its value is making implicit judgements explicit.

answer.text: Digital collation tools cannot process non-Latin scripts like Polytonic Greek.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CollateX and modern tools handle Greek and UTF-8 encoded scripts cleanly when configured.

answer.text: Funding agencies require a hand-written collation card archive for every digital edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. There is no such requirement; the exercise is methodological and pedagogical.

questiontext.text: What is the primary procedural challenge encountered when collating two texts manually word by word?

generalfeedback.text: Re-establishing alignment after an omission is the hard part by hand — and it is exactly what Wednesday's algorithm computes.

answer.text: Re-establishing alignment and resynchronizing the texts after encountering an omission or addition.

feedback.text: Correct. After an omission, the two texts fall out of step, requiring careful counting and scanning to find where they re-align.

answer.text: Translating every foreign lexeme into English before recording its spelling.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Collation records verbatim readings and locations, not real-time translation.

answer.text: Ensuring that both manuscripts use the exact same page dimensions and ruling lines.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Codicological physical layout does not need to match across witnesses during collation.

answer.text: Converting all Greek characters to ASCII transliterations on the recording sheet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Readings are recorded verbatim in their authentic polytonic script.

questiontext.text: Why do orthographic variants carry much lower genealogical value than long omissions or lexical substitutions?

generalfeedback.text: Orthographic variants are weak evidence because two scribes can produce them independently; long omissions are strong evidence because they cannot.

answer.text: Orthographic variants are polygenetic and can be produced independently by multiple scribes sharing period phonology, whereas identical long omissions rarely occur by chance.

feedback.text: Correct. Independent convergence is common in spelling (e.g., iotacism), whereas a specific lexical replacement or substantial omission points strongly to a shared ancestor.

answer.text: Orthographic variants cannot be encoded within TEI critical apparatus elements.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI encodes all types of variants; the distinction is genealogical and philological, not technical.

answer.text: Omissions and substitutions are always intentional, while spelling changes are always accidental.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Omissions are frequently mechanical errors (homoioteleuton), yet still carry very high stemmatic value.

answer.text: Orthographic variants only occur in printed editions, never in handwritten manuscripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manuscript transmission is saturated with orthographic variation due to phonological evolution.

questiontext.text: How does the mechanism of homoioteleuton explain why omissions often form single extended gaps rather than scattered mismatches?

generalfeedback.text: Check every omission's boundaries for similar endings — homoioteleuton is a single cognitive event, which is why Wednesday's algorithm penalizes gap opening rather than gap length.

answer.text: A scribe's eye skips from one word ending to an identical or similar ending further down the page, dropping the intervening passage in a single cognitive lapse.

feedback.text: Correct. The skip occurs in one glance, which is why Gotoh's affine gap penalty models it as an open gap with low extension cost.

answer.text: A scribe deliberately censors theological passages by systematically altering word endings across adjacent lines.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Homoioteleuton is a mechanical visual error caused by similar endings, not deliberate censorship.

answer.text: Physical ink degradation causes the parchment to lose legibility at fixed mathematical intervals.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Homoioteleuton is a cognitive copying error, not physical damage to the carrier.

answer.text: The binding of the exemplar drops several leaves simultaneously whenever a quire is restitched.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lost leaves cause large codicological lacunae, whereas homoioteleuton is an eye-skip between similar words.

questiontext.text: Why do textual transpositions present a fundamental mathematical challenge for variant graph models like CollateX?

generalfeedback.text: Mark transpositions distinctly — Wednesday's algorithm will report each as a separate omission and addition, and your record is what shows that is wrong.

answer.text: The variant graph must remain a directed acyclic graph (DAG) to preserve linear reading order, so drawing a backward edge to moved text would create a forbidden cycle.

feedback.text: Correct. Traversal algorithms would loop infinitely on a cyclic graph, forcing CollateX to handle transpositions via secondary heuristics rather than primary graph edges.

answer.text: Transpositions alter the total character count of the file, invalidating UTF-8 checksums.

feedback.text: Incorrect. UTF-8 checksums are irrelevant to sequence alignment logic.

answer.text: Dynamic programming matrices cannot compute alignment scores if words contain more than two syllables.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Dynamic programming operates on token sequences regardless of syllable length.

answer.text: Transpositions can only occur in modern printed editions, so classical algorithms never supported them.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transpositions are common scribal errors and editorial rearrangements in ancient manuscripts.

questiontext.text: Why is maintaining a systematic list of discounted differences just as crucial as recording genuine variants?

generalfeedback.text: The list of differences you discount becomes Wednesday's configuration — and its length measures how much manual collation relies on implicit knowledge.

answer.text: The discounted list specifies the exact normalization rules needed to prevent automated alignment algorithms from generating massive noise.

feedback.text: Correct. Left unconfigured, an algorithm flags every minor capitalization or spelling difference as a substantive variant; the discounted list is the algorithm's configuration specification.

answer.text: Discounted differences must be submitted to the publisher to justify deletion of manuscript witnesses.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Witnesses are not deleted; discounted differences are simply neutralized during substantive collation.

answer.text: It proves to funding bodies that the manual collation required more hours than computational alignment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The discounted list serves a technical and editorial purpose, not a funding audit.

answer.text: Moodle question banks require every discounted item to be formatted as a true/false quiz question.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The discounted list is used for configuring alignment tools, not quiz generation.

questiontext.text: What is the technical and evidential trade-off between stripping punctuation and tokenizing it separately during collation?

generalfeedback.text: Decide punctuation handling from what your witnesses actually do — stripping absent punctuation costs nothing, stripping meaningful punctuation costs evidence.

answer.text: Stripping punctuation simplifies alignment but discards historical evidence of how scribes parsed syntax; tokenizing it preserves evidence at the cost of expanding graph size.

feedback.text: Correct. Punctuation carries historical interpretation, but separate tokens enlarge the variant graph and attached punctuation creates spurious lexical mismatches.

answer.text: Stripping punctuation causes dynamic programming matrices to enter infinite recursion loops.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Stripping punctuation simplifies the matrix; it does not cause recursion errors.

answer.text: Tokenizing punctuation makes it impossible to detect substantive lexical substitutions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lexical substitutions are still detected; only the graph dimensions increase.

answer.text: TEI guidelines strictly prohibit encoding punctuation marks inside apparatus entries.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI allows punctuation within apparatus readings if the editor chooses to record it.

name.text: 12 Question: Case Study: The Canterbury Tales Project

questiontext.text: How did Peter Robinson's Canterbury Tales Project transform manual collation data into genealogical stemmata?

generalfeedback.text: Phylogenetic stemmatics consumes collation data as its input — the variant record you are building by hand is what those methods run on.

answer.text: By applying phylogenetic algorithms from evolutionary biology (such as maximum parsimony and neighbour-joining) to distance matrices computed from collation data.

feedback.text: Correct. The project treated scribal copies with modification as analogous to biological evolution with mutation, constructing unrooted phylogenetic trees from collation metrics.

answer.text: By using optical character recognition to replace all manual transcriptions with machine vision models.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The breakthrough was applying biological phylogenetic software to structured collation data.

answer.text: By declaring that all fifty-five surviving manuscripts descended from a single lost 1476 Caxton print.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The project mapped manuscript traditions using evolutionary distance, not a simplistic Caxton derivation.

answer.text: By proving that manual index cards produce stemmata with zero error compared to automated graphs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Robinson moved away from Manly & Rickert's manual index card system to automated digital alignment.

name.text: 13 Question: Case Study: The Editio Critica Maior and Contamination

questiontext.text: Why does textual contamination in the Greek New Testament tradition break classical Lachmannian stemmatics?

generalfeedback.text: Contamination breaks tree models, and Greek biblical traditions are heavily contaminated — do not over-interpret a two-witness collation as clean descent.

answer.text: Contamination occurs when scribes consult multiple exemplars, creating a textual network with multiple parents that cannot be modeled as a single branching tree.

feedback.text: Correct. Lachmannian stemmata assume each witness has exactly one parent; when traditions cross-pollinate, tree models collapse and require network methods like the CBGM.

answer.text: Contamination introduces physical chemical mold onto parchment, preventing multispectral imaging.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Textual contamination is the genealogical mixture of readings from different exemplars, not physical mold.

answer.text: Contaminated traditions contain zero substantive variants, making collation unnecessary.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Contaminated traditions contain vast numbers of competing substantive variants.

answer.text: Lachmannian stemmatics was designed exclusively for vernacular Romance languages rather than ancient Greek.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lachmann's method was developed on classical Latin and Greek texts, but assumes uncontaminated stemma trees.

questiontext.text: During manual collation, what does a continuous stretch of five or more lines with zero recorded variants often indicate?

generalfeedback.text: A long run with no variants may mean lost alignment rather than agreement — check before trusting it.

answer.text: The editor may have lost parallel alignment between the witnesses rather than discovered perfect agreement.

feedback.text: Correct. When texts fall out of step, an editor can easily scan past differences unnoticed; long stretches of agreement should be checked for alignment integrity.

answer.text: The two manuscripts were undeniably copied by the exact same historical scribe on the same day.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scribes copying different exemplars rarely agree verbatim for long stretches without close kinship, but lost alignment must be ruled out first.

answer.text: The text has transitioned from prose into metrical poetry.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Verse passages also contain scribal variation; zero variants suggests possible missed alignment.

answer.text: The transcription file has been corrupted by an unclosed XML tag.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manual paper collation involves visual inspection, not XML parser crashes.

questiontext.text: In the structured JSON format for manual collation, why are variant locations recorded separately for both Witness A and Witness B?

generalfeedback.text: Record discounted differences alongside variants — they are Wednesday's configuration, not merely notes.

answer.text: Because additions, omissions, and different layout formats cause the same variant site to appear at different folio, line, and word positions in each witness.

feedback.text: Correct. Each witness has its own codicological coordinates; recording both is essential for verifying alignment and citations.

answer.text: Because JSON schemas require redundant location keys to satisfy valid XML conversion constraints.

feedback.text: Incorrect. JSON schemas are designed by the editor; dual coordinates reflect codicological reality, not XML constraints.

answer.text: Because Witness A is always assumed to be in Greek and Witness B in Latin translation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both witnesses are manuscripts of the same passage, but with different pagination and lineation.

answer.text: Because Git merge drivers will corrupt files that do not maintain mirrored key-value pairs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git tracks text lines; recording both locations allows human and algorithmic verification.

name.text: 16 Question: Writing the Collation Method Document

questiontext.text: Why must the collation method document (collation/METHOD.md) be written immediately after manual collation rather than postponed?

generalfeedback.text: Every imprecise line in the method document becomes a default you accept under time pressure tomorrow.

answer.text: Every tacit decision left unrecorded becomes an arbitrary default accepted under time pressure when configuring automated tools.

feedback.text: Correct. Capturing discounting rules, tokenization policies, and taxonomy criteria while fresh ensures automated alignment is properly specified.

answer.text: Late submission of markdown method files triggers automated penalties in the TEI validation suite.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI validation checks XML schema compliance, not the timestamp of your markdown method notes.

answer.text: CollateX cannot execute unless it parses a compiled Markdown documentation header at runtime.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CollateX is configured via Python scripts or JSON input, not by reading METHOD.md directly.

answer.text: Method documents must be registered with the GitHub API before branch merging is permitted.

feedback.text: Incorrect. METHOD.md is an editorial specification for reproducibility, not a GitHub API requirement.

name.text: 17 Question: What the Manual Method Gives You

questiontext.text: What capability does manual collation provide that deterministic alignment algorithms completely lack?

generalfeedback.text: Manual collation supplies interpretation and classification that the algorithm cannot; the algorithm supplies scale and reproducibility that you cannot.

answer.text: Continuous contextual interpretation, allowing the scholar to evaluate syntactic sense, recognize transpositions as single events, and classify variant significance.

feedback.text: Correct. Human editors understand meaning, recognizing why a scribe made a mistake or that moved text is one event, whereas algorithms simply calculate string differences.

answer.text: The ability to collate millions of words across hundreds of witnesses without fatigue error.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scaling to millions of words without fatigue is the distinct advantage of automated collation, not manual work.

answer.text: Exact, mathematically reproducible output that never varies across repetitions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manual collation varies with human attention and fatigue; algorithms provide strict reproducibility.

answer.text: Automatic extraction of RGB channel layers from multispectral IIIF manifests.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Multispectral image processing is an imaging workflow, not manual collation.

questiontext.text: Why is it essential to install and test CollateX in your Python environment prior to the automated collation workshop?

generalfeedback.text: Install and test CollateX before Wednesday — installation failures are the commonest way to lose the session.

answer.text: Environment and dependency installation issues are the most frequent cause of lost workshop time and can be resolved in advance.

feedback.text: Correct. Testing imports and trivial collation runs beforehand ensures class time is spent on algorithm configuration and philological analysis.

answer.text: CollateX requires a 24-hour background indexing job before processing its first text file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CollateX aligns short texts in fractions of a second without background pre-indexing.

answer.text: Python packages cannot be installed on Linux workstations once a git repository is initialized.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Package installation via pip is independent of git repository status.

answer.text: CollateX licenses must be verified against an institutional proxy server every morning.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CollateX is an open-source library requiring no proprietary license verification.

questiontext.text: If a manual collation between two witnesses reveals zero omissions and zero transpositions, what should the editor conclude?

generalfeedback.text: Finding no omissions or transpositions is a finding about your witnesses' relationship, not a failed exercise.

answer.text: The absence of complex variance is itself an informative finding indicating a close genealogical relationship between the witnesses.

feedback.text: Correct. Close witnesses may differ only in minor orthographic or morphological ways; lack of dramatic errors is valuable genealogical evidence.

answer.text: The collation has failed and must be repeated from scratch on an entirely different chapter.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A clean or closely matching textual transmission is a valid historical finding, not a failure.

answer.text: The editor must fabricate an omission to properly test Wednesday's alignment algorithm.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editors never invent fake manuscript readings in authentic editions.

answer.text: The witnesses must be discarded because identical texts cannot be encoded in TEI XML.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Close witnesses are easily encoded and provide valuable confirmation of textual stability.

questiontext.text: If a preliminary manual or automated extraction reports disagreement at virtually every single word position, what is the most probable cause?

generalfeedback.text: Disagreement everywhere usually means a broken extraction, and agreement everywhere usually means either close kinship or lost alignment — verify before concluding.

answer.text: A broken extraction pipeline that concatenated both and layers or failed to align the passage starting point.

feedback.text: Correct. Pervasive disagreement across the entire text almost always points to an extraction error (like unstripped dual tags) or misaligned start tokens.

answer.text: The two scribes were writing in completely different dialects of ancient Greek that share no vocabulary.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Witnesses of the same passage share vocabulary; total mismatch indicates a technical alignment or extraction breakdown.

answer.text: The Greek Unicode polytonic text was converted into Latin ASCII hex codes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hex code conversion would corrupt characters visibly, but extraction concatenation is the common failure.

answer.text: The manuscript exemplar was written in a non-linear boustrophedon layout.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Medieval Greek manuscripts are not written boustrophedon; the issue is pipeline preprocessing.

name.text: 21 Question: What Good Work Looks Like Here

questiontext.text: What distinguishes high-quality philological collation from a mere mechanical list of differences?

generalfeedback.text: Recording that an omission is bounded by similar endings turns a datum into an interpretation — and changes what the variant is evidence for.

answer.text: Evaluating the mechanism and context of variants — such as checking omission boundaries for homoioteleuton to distinguish mechanical skips from deliberate edits.

feedback.text: Correct. Scholarship transforms raw differences into evidence by analyzing scribal mechanisms, syntactic context, and genealogical significance.

answer.text: Ensuring that every single spelling variation is printed in bold red ink in the final apparatus.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Good work exercises editorial filtering rather than highlighting noise with typography.

answer.text: Replacing all Latin grammatical terminology with modern computational software terms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Traditional philological analysis remains the interpretive framework for understanding textual descent.

answer.text: Rejecting all computational tools in favor of hand-written index cards.

feedback.text: Incorrect. High-quality work combines rigorous manual analysis with computational alignment.

name.text: 22 Question: Two Witnesses and Its Limits

questiontext.text: Why is it generally impossible to determine which reading is original when collating exactly two witnesses?

generalfeedback.text: Two witnesses record variation and cannot generally determine which reading is original — state that limit rather than overreaching.

answer.text: Without a third independent witness or external genealogical structure, there is no majority reading to break ties between competing grammatical variants.

feedback.text: Correct. With two witnesses, one can record differences and analyze scribal habits, but establishing originality requires broader witness evidence or strong internal criteria.

answer.text: Two witnesses cannot be compared using dynamic programming matrices.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pairwise comparison is precisely what dynamic programming does best.

answer.text: TEI critical apparatus modules require a minimum of five witnesses before validating XML syntax.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI schemas validate apparatus entries with two or more readings.

answer.text: Copyright law prohibits establishing priority between fewer than three historical artifacts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical manuscripts are in the public domain; the limitation is purely stemmatic.

name.text: 23 Question: Genetic Editing: A Different Application

questiontext.text: How does genetic editing apply collation tools like CollateX to modern authorial manuscripts?

generalfeedback.text: Treating drafts as witnesses makes the same machinery trace authorial revision — and your own Git history is a genetic edition of your edition.

answer.text: By treating successive authorial drafts and revision campaigns as distinct witnesses to trace the development of a text over time.

feedback.text: Correct. In genetic editions (e.g., Darwin or Beckett projects), drafts represent temporal layers within the creation process rather than scribal copying errors.

answer.text: By sequencing the biological DNA of the author from hair samples left on the manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Genetic editing is the study of textual genesis and authorial revision, not biological genome sequencing.

answer.text: By automatically deleting all rejected authorial revisions to produce an unblemished clean text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Genetic criticism preserves and visualizes every layer of expansion, deletion, and revision.

answer.text: By proving that modern authors never revise their texts once a first draft is completed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Modern authorial manuscripts are characterized by intense, multi-layered revision campaigns.

questiontext.text: Why must an editor establish a clear variant taxonomy and filtering policy before generating Week 8's critical apparatus?

generalfeedback.text: Your taxonomy determines what enters Week 8's apparatus — including everything makes it unreadable, so the filtering policy must be stated.

answer.text: An apparatus containing every trivial orthographic variation is practically unreadable, so the editor must define which tiers are reported in the main apparatus.

feedback.text: Correct. Critical editions filter out non-substantive noise so readers can focus on meaningful lexical, morphological, and structural variation.

answer.text: The TEI apparatus module crashes if an edition contains more than ten total variant entries.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI handles thousands of entries; filtering is an editorial readability necessity.

answer.text: Orthographic variants are legally protected under fair dealing exceptions and cannot be published.

feedback.text: Incorrect. There are no copyright restrictions on ancient manuscript spelling variants.

answer.text: Moodle question banks only support multiple-choice questions based on lexical substitutions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Question banks can test any topic; apparatus filtering is a scholarly standard.

name.text: 25 Question: Synthesis: The Judgement Behind the Comparison

questiontext.text: In what sense does automated collation NOT perform the textual criticism for the editor?

generalfeedback.text: Automated collation produces the dataset on which criticism is performed; today's judgements are the criticism, and they are what the tool must be told.

answer.text: The algorithm only aligns character strings according to rules it is given; defining what counts as a variant, classifying its type, and interpreting its descent remain human judgements.

feedback.text: Correct. Automation creates a mathematically rigorous dataset, but textual criticism consists of the philological interpretation performed upon that data.

answer.text: Automated collation produces corrupt binary output that cannot be read by human scholars.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CollateX exports standard tables, CSV, DOT graphs, and TEI XML.

answer.text: Algorithms cannot execute unless an editor manually approves every single word match in real time.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Algorithms run autonomously once configured; the human role is configuration, classification, and evaluation.

answer.text: Textual criticism is concerned solely with measuring physical ink weight rather than variant readings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Textual criticism evaluates textual variation and transmission history.

name.text: 26 Question: A Note on Fatigue and Reliability

questiontext.text: When automated collation identifies a variant in your text that was not present in your manual collation record, how should it be evaluated?

generalfeedback.text: Wednesday will find variants you missed through fatigue — treat those as findings rather than as the tool's false positives.

answer.text: As a potential genuine variant missed during manual collation due to human fatigue, which should be verified against the manuscript facsimile.

feedback.text: Correct. Machine attention is uniform and indefatigable; discrepancies should be investigated as valuable corrections rather than reflexively dismissed as tool errors.

answer.text: As an unrecoverable software glitch caused by processor overheating.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Deterministic algorithms execute logic faithfully; novel variants are often human omissions.

answer.text: As proof that the digital image of the manuscript was altered during download.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Image files remain constant; human attention lapses during repetitive manual comparison.

answer.text: As a hallucination generated by the compiler's neural network cache.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CollateX is a deterministic sequence alignment engine, not a generative language model.

name.text: 27 Question: Estimating What Automation Must Suppress

questiontext.text: Why is comparing the count of discounted differences against recorded variants a useful diagnostic before running automated collation?

generalfeedback.text: Predict tomorrow's raw difference count from your discounted list — a large discrepancy means either your list is incomplete or the tool tokenizes differently than you assume.

answer.text: The ratio predicts the expected signal-to-noise ratio and establishes a baseline for how aggressively the normalization pipeline must filter non-substantive variance.

feedback.text: Correct. If discounted differences far outnumber variants, an unconfigured run will produce massive noise; predicting the count tests your understanding of the pipeline.

answer.text: If the count of discounted differences is odd, the collation algorithm will throw a division-by-zero error.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Sequence alignment algorithms do not depend on even numbers of discounted tokens.

answer.text: A high count of discounted differences proves that the manuscript was forged in the Renaissance.

feedback.text: Incorrect. High orthographic variation reflects natural linguistic evolution and scribal phonology.

answer.text: It allows the editor to calculate the exact monetary cost of cloud GPU computing hours.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CollateX runs locally on a standard CPU with negligible computational cost.

questiontext.text: Why is rejoining words split across line breaks an essential preprocessing step in manuscript tokenization?

generalfeedback.text: Rejoin words broken across lines before tokenizing, or your witnesses will differ wherever their line breaks fall differently.

answer.text: Witnesses break lines at different places, so treating hyphenated fragments as separate tokens would create spurious variant mismatches at every single line ending.

feedback.text: Correct. Lineation is an artifact of page layout; failing to rejoin words fractures the alignment at every line break.

answer.text: Greek grammatical syntax prohibits words from having more than seven letters on a single line.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Greek words can be of any length; scribes split words across lines according to syllabic rules.

answer.text: Unicode NFC normalization automatically strips all line breaks from XML documents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. NFC normalizes character compositions; it does not remove line break elements or newlines.

answer.text: CollateX cannot parse files containing whitespace characters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CollateX splits on whitespace by default; the problem is words broken into two separate chunks.

questiontext.text: Why are half of the outputs produced during manual collation actually specifications for Wednesday's automated alignment rather than finished results?

generalfeedback.text: Half of today's outputs are configuration for tomorrow rather than results — the manual step specifies the automation as well as providing the reference.

answer.text: Because defining tokens, discount rules, normalization layers, and baseline expectations provides the exact configuration required to run automated collation meaningfully.

feedback.text: Correct. The manual step produces both a verification reference and the explicit rule specification needed to configure algorithmic alignment.

answer.text: Because manual collation records are discarded as soon as the student leaves the classroom.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The manual record is committed and tagged as the benchmark against which automation is evaluated.

answer.text: Because digital tools refuse to execute unless fed hand-written paper notes via a scanner.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tools consume digital configuration files (JSON/Python) derived from manual analysis.

answer.text: Because the university examination board requires half of all coursework to be stored in physical binders.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The dual output reflects the relationship between human ground truth and machine configuration.

name.text: 30 Question: Synthesis: Recording Difference, Interpreting Descent

questiontext.text: What is the ultimate relationship between recording textual differences and interpreting textual descent?

generalfeedback.text: Collation produces evidence for inferences about descent, and the inferences depend on a classification only judgement supplies.

answer.text: Recording differences creates the necessary dataset, but determining genealogical descent depends entirely on qualitative variant classification and philological judgement.

feedback.text: Correct. Data collection is the foundation, but inferences about stemmatic trees or textual flow require analyzing which variants represent shared ancestral errors.

answer.text: Recording differences automatically generates an infallible stemma without requiring variant classification.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Raw difference counts conflate polygenetic spelling with stemmatic errors, leading to erroneous stemmata.
